sec.title: Background
sec.p: Emerging clinical and mouse tumor data indicate that tumor cells induce immune suppression in an anatomical site-specific manner. In lung metastases, tumor cell programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) engages myeloid cell programmed cell death protein 1 to activate SHP2 to suppress type I interferon (IFN-I) expression to repress Cxcl9 expression to impair cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) tumor recruitment. Loss of IFN-I expression thus underlies tumor immune evasion in lung metastases niche. We aimed at testing the hypothesis that forcing tumor cells to express IFNα2 activates Cxcl9 expression to increase CTL tumor recruitment to suppress lung metastasis.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Codon usage-optimized IFNα2-encoding DNA was designed and cloned to plasmid. IFNα2-encoding messenger RNA (mRNA) was synthesized. The plasmid DNA and mRNA were encapsulated into DOTAP (N-[1-(2,3-Dioleoyloxy)propyl]-N,N,N-trimethylammonium methyl-sulfate)-cholesterol to generate lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated mouse IFNα2 (LNP-mIFNα2), human IFNα2 plasmid, and mouse IFNα2 mRNA (LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA). Mouse breast tumor spontaneous lung metastasis, mouse melanoma experimental lung metastasis, and human colon tumor experimental lung metastasis humanized mouse models were used to determine LNP-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid and mRNA efficacy in IFNα2 expression and antitumor immunity, toxicity, and mechanism of action in vivo.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: LNP-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid primarily accumulated in tumor-bearing lungs in mice. LNP-IFNα2 therapy produces mouse IFNα2 protein in mouse tumor-bearing mice and human IFNα2 protein in human tumor-bearing humanized mice to suppress lung metastasis, respectively. Similarly, LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA therapy produces mouse IFNα2 protein and suppressed lung metastasis in tumor-bearing mice. The increased IFNα2 protein activates Cxcl9 expression and increases T cell infiltration in lung metastases. LNP-IFNα2 therapy did not induce liver toxicity and inflammatory cytokines. In human patients with cancer, IFN-I pathway activation is correlated with CXCL9 expression and T cell expansion after PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy. Mechanistically, LNP-delivered IFNα2 suppresses tumor lung metastasis through upregulating Cxcl9 in tumor-bearing mice.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our findings determine that LNP-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid DNA and mRNA are effective agents in restoring IFNα2 expression to activate Cxcl9 expression to enhance T cell tumor recruitment to suppress tumor lung metastasis. LNP-IFNα2 is potentially a safe and yet effective third-generation IFNα2 agent for human cancer immunotherapy to treat patients with lung metastasis.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Emerging literature indicates that tumor cell programmed death-ligand 1 engages myeloid cell programmed cell death protein 1 to activate SHP2 to antagonize type I interferon (IFN-I) expression to repress Cxcl9 expression to suppress cytotoxic T lymphocyte recruitment to promote tumor lung metastasis. Loss of IFN-I expression and function therefore underlies tumor cell immune evasion and resultant lung metastasis. The current approved IFN-I agent is the exogenous recombinant IFNα2 protein that exhibits severe adverse effects.

We have developed cationic lipid nanoparticle (LNP) DOTAP (N-[1-(2,3-Dioleoyloxy)propyl]-N,N,N-trimethylammonium methyl-sulfate)-cholesterol-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid DNA and messenger RNA (mRNA). LNP delivery of IFNα2-encoding plasmid produced endogenous IFNα2 protein in mouse tumor lung metastases and humanized tumor lung metastases to suppress metastasis in mice and humanized mice, respectively. LNP-encapsulated IFNα2 mRNA also produces endogenous IFNα2 protein to suppress tumor lung metastasis in mice. Mechanistically, LNP-delivered IFNα2-encoding plasmid suppresses tumor lung metastasis at least in part through up-regulating Cxcl9 expression to increase T cell tumor recruitment.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: Lung metastases are the second most common metastatic disease for patients with cancer and occur in approximately 30% of patients with cancer with metastatic cancer. Our findings indicate that LNP-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid and mRNA are potentially the third generation of effective and safe IFNα2 agent for lung metastases immunotherapy.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) is an inhibitory ligand that directly engages its co-inhibitory receptor programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) expressed on cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) to induce SHP2 phosphorylation. Phosphorylation activates SHP2 that dephosphorylates both the T cell receptor (TCR) and the T cell costimulatory receptor CD281 to inhibit TCR and CD28-initiated signaling cascades, driving CTLs into a dysfunctional and exhausted state. The PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy therefore acts through blocking the interaction between PD-L1 and PD-1 to reinvigorate the dysfunctional and exhausted CTLs, leading to active anti-tumor cytotoxicity and resultant tumor suppression.2 The PD-L1 and PD-1 immunosuppressive axis therefore serves as a direct molecular shield against CTL cytotoxicity toward the target tumor cells.3 While this direct PD-L1 and CTL PD-1 engagement plays a key role in CTL immune suppression in human patients with cancer and tumor-bearing mice, emerging experimental data has highlighted the importance of PD-1 expression in other cell populations, particularly in myeloid cells, in tumor immune evasion.46 We have recently determined that tumor cell PD-L1 engages myeloid cell PD-1 to activate SHP2 to antagonize the type I interferon (IFN-I)/STAT1 pathway to repress Cxcl9 expression in myeloid cells to suppress CTL tumor recruitment to promote tumor lung metastasis.7 This finding indicates that PD-L1-induced loss of IFN-I expression is a key determinant of lung metastases immune escape and IFN-I is a molecular target of tumor lung metastases therapy. Restoring IFN-I expression and function therefore is expected to activate Cxcl9 expression to enhance CTL tumor infiltration to suppress tumor lung metastasis.

IFNα2 protein is a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved agent for human cancer.8 High dose and high administration frequency are required to achieve therapeutic responses due to its short half-life, which is associated with severe adverse effects. To overcome adverse effects, polymer polyethylene glycol was conjugated to recombinant IFNα2 protein.9 These second-generation IFNα2 proteins (Pegasys and PegIntron) have a longer half-life with increased efficacy.912 However, there is no overall significant decrease in adverse effects.13 Masked IFN-I has also been created to target tumor sites for tumor cell protease-dependent release to increase half-life and to reduce toxicity. However, the active agent is still exogenous recombinant IFN-I protein.14

The success of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated COVID-19 messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine represents a breakthrough in nucleic acid-based therapy for a human disease.15 Similarly, protein-encoding plasmid DNA has been encapsulated to LNP and administered to human patients with cancer and tumor-bearing mice to produce a tumor suppressor protein.1619 DOTAP (N-[1-(2,3-Dioleoyloxy)propyl]-N,N,N-trimethylammonium methyl-sulfate)-cholesterol is a cationic LNP that has been shown to be effective in delivering plasmid DNA to tumor cells in human patients with cancer without significant toxicity.16 There are currently three DOTAP-cholesterol-plasmid clinical trials in patients with cancer (NCT05703971, NCT05062980, NCT04486833). We aimed at testing the hypothesis that LNP delivery of IFNα2-encoding plasmid DNA and mRNA is effective in transfecting tumor cells to force tumor cells to express IFNα2 to activate Cxcl9 to enhance CTL tumor recruitment to suppress lung metastasis.

sec.title: Tumor cell lines
sec.p: The murine mammary carcinoma cell line 4T1 and melanoma cell line B16-F10 were obtained from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, Virginia, USA) in 2022. The human colon carcinoma cell line SW620 was obtained from ATCC in 2019. The original ATCC tumor cell lines were stored as aliquots in liquid nitrogen. Each aliquot was used less than 30 passages and discarded. All tumor cells were tested bi-monthly for mycoplasma contamination and all cells were mycoplasma-negative at the time of the experiments.

sec.title: Human blood specimens
sec.p: Human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were obtained from Shepeard Community Blood Center (Augusta, Georgia, USA) from consented and de-identified healthy donors. Use of deidentified human PBMCs was approved by Augusta University Institute Review Board (Approval # 1354508–1) and determined as non-human subject research.

sec.title: Human patient datasets
sec.p: Human breast cancer single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq) datasets were downloaded from the European Genome–phenome Archive (EGA, study # EGAS00001004809 and accession # EGAD0000100660820). Human melanoma scRNA-Seq datasets were downloaded from Gene Expression Omnibus under accession # GSE115978.21 The datasets were analyzed using R package.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle
sec.p: The cationic LNP DOTAP-cholesterol (1:1 molar ratio) was synthesized, produced, and quality control-tested (online supplemental table S1) in T&T Scientific Corp (Knoxville, Tennessee, USA) and provided by Genprex (Austin, Texas, USA).

sec.title: IFNα2 plasmid DNA
sec.p: Codon usage-optimized mouse and human IFNα2 cDNA were designed and synthesized using the GeneArt algorithm (Fisher Thermal Scientific).22 The synthesized mouse and human codon usage-optimized DNA fragments were cloned to nanoplasmid NTC9385R23 to generate NTC9385R-mIFNα2 and NTC9385R-hIFNα2 plasmids, respectively, at Aldevron (Fargo, North Dakota, USA). Large-scale NTC9385R-mIFNα2 and NTC9385R-hIFNα2 plasmid production and quality control tests were carried out in Aldevron.

sec.title: IFNα2 mRNA
sec.p: The mouse IFNα2 mRNA was produced in TriLink BioTechnologies (San Diego, California, USA). The codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2-coding DNA was chemically synthesized with N1-methylpseudouridine base modification and cloned to the T7 expression vector. IFNα2 mRNA was synthesized using the T7 RNA polymerase in vitro transcription system. The synthesized mRNA was capped with cleancap M6, added a 120 amino acid poly A tail, and purified in silica membrane. The A260/A280 ratio is 2.05. Fragment analyzer and gel electrophoresis confirmed the mRNA size and integrity. The endotoxin level is <0.5 EU/mg RNA.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle-encapsulation of plasmid and mRNA
sec.p: To formulate LNP-encapsulated DNA and mRNA, DOTAP-cholesterol, plasmid DNA, and mRNA were diluted in 5% Dextrose (Cat # 76313–652, VWR International) to 25 µg/mouse or 5 µg/mouse, respectively. The diluted DOTAP-cholesterol (4 mM) was then mixed with plasmid DNA or mRNA in 1:1 molar ratio, incubated at room temperature for 30 min to formulate mouse IFNα2-encoding plasmid (LNP-mIFNα2), human IFNα2-encoding plasmid (LNP-hIFNα2), and mouse IFNα2-encoding mRNA (LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA). The liposomes were characterized by using a scanning microscope to determine particle morphology and size.

sec.title: Characterization of plasmid DNA and mRNA-encapsulated lipid nanoparticle
sec.p: For Zeta potential, LNP-mIFNα2, LNP-hIFNα2, and LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA were diluted in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and analyzed using an automatic particle size detector (Zetasizer Nano ZS, Malvern, UK). For hydrodynamic diameter and Polydispersity Index, the nanoparticles dispersed in PBS were characterized by dynamic light scattering using Zetasizer Nano ZS. Z-average is calculated as the intensity-weighted average hydrodynamic size of the nanoparticle.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle encapsulation efficiency
sec.p: Encapsulation efficiency was determined by iQuant RiboGreen RNA Assay Kit (ABP Bioscience, Rockville, Maryland, USA). LNP-mIFNα2, LNP-hIFNα2, and LNP-IFNα2 mRNA were prepared as described above, incubated with Triton-X100 at a 1% final concentration for 10 min at room temperature to degrade the nanoparticle to release the encapsulated nucleic acid. RiboGreen was added to the untreated nanoparticle (for free/unencapsulated mRNA or plasmid DNA measurement) and the Triton-X100-treated nanoparticle (for total mRNA or plasmid DNA measurement), respectively, at a 1:1 ratio in a black opaque 96-well plate. Fluorescence measurements (λex=480 nm, λem=520 nm) were collected with BioTek Cytation 5-plate reader and Gen5 V.3.10 software (Agilent Tech, Santa Clara, California, USA). Encapsulation efficiency was calculated as percentages of total mRNA or plasmid DNA—free mRNA or plasmid DNA over total mRNA or total plasmid DNA.

sec.title: Mice and tumor-bearing mouse models
sec.p: BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice were obtained from Charles River Laboratories at National Cancer Institute at Frederick (Frederick, Maryland, USA). NSG mice were obtained from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA). To establish a primary tumor with a spontaneous breast cancer mouse model, 4T1 cells (2×104 cell/mouse) were injected into the #3 mammary gland of female BALB/c mice. To establish a breast cancer experimental lung metastasis mouse model, 4T1 cells (2×104 cells/mouse) were intravenously injected into the tail vein of female BALB/c mice. B16-F10 tumor cells were originated from a male C57BL/6 mice. To establish a melanoma experimental lung metastasis mouse model, B16-F10 cells (5×105 cells/mouse) were injected intravenously into the tail vein of male C57BL/6 mice. Tumor size was measured with a digital caliper. Tumor weight was measured by weighing the dissected tumor. Tumor lung metastases were analyzed by injecting India ink (10% India ink in 0.1% ammonium hydroxide and 89.9% water) into the lungs via the trachea. The inflated lungs were washed briefly in water and fixed in Fekete’s fixation solution (50% ethanol, 6% formaldehyde, and 3% glacial acetic acid). Tumor nodules were examined and quantified. For histological analysis, tissues were fixed in 10% formalin and embedded in paraffin. The sections were stained with H&E in the Medical College of Georgia Electron Microscopy and Histology Core Facility. All mouse studies were approved by Augusta University Institute Animal Care and Use Committee (Approval # 2008–0162). The live tumor size limit is 2000 mm3 and the body weight loss limit is 15%, whichever comes first. In rare cases, the live tumor size exceeded 2000 mm3 due to the difficulty in accurately monitoring tumor size under the skin in live mice. Once the tumor size was found to exceed 2000 mm3, the tumor-bearing mouse was sacrificed on the same day.

sec.title: Human tumor humanized mouse model
sec.p: NSG mice were injected intravenously with human PBMCs (3×106 cells/mouse) as previously described.18 Human colon SW620 tumor cells (3×106 cells/mouse) were then injected intravenously to the humanized mice to establish the experimental lung metastasis mouse model. Tumor lung metastases were analyzed by injecting India ink (10% India ink in 0.1% ammonium hydroxide and 89.9% water) into the lungs via the trachea. The inflated lungs were washed briefly in water and fixed in Fekete’s fixation solution (50% ethanol, 6% formaldehyde, and 3% glacial acetic acid).

sec.title: Analysis of tumor-infiltrating T cells
sec.p: For tumor-infiltrating immune cell analysis, dissected tumors were digested in collagenase solution (1 mg/mL collagenase (Sigma-Aldrich, Missouri, USA), 0.1 mg/mL hyaluronidase (Sigma-Aldrich), and 30 U/mL DNase I (Fisher Scientific)). The digest was passed through a 100 µM cell strainer (Corning, Corning, New York, USA), lysed with red cell lysis buffer, stained with fluorescent dye-conjugated CD4-specific and CD8-specific monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) (BioLegend, San Diego, California, USA), and analyzed on a FACSCalibur cell analyzer. All flow cytometry data was analyzed with FlowJo V.10.10.0 (BD Biosciences).

sec.title: Detection of codon usage-optimized IFNα2 expression
sec.p: The codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2-encoding DNA sequence and human IFNα2-encoding DNA sequence were used to design PCR primers, respectively. The wild-type (wt) mouse and human IFNα2 complementary DNA (cDNA) sequences were used as references to select primers that have maximal mismatch with the wt IFNα2 cDNA sequence. The PCR primers for codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2 are: forward: 5'-GAACCTGTTCACCAGCAAAGC-3', reverse: 5'-GCTCAGGGCTCTCCAAACTTC-3'. The PCR primers for wt mouse IFNα2 are: forward: 5'-CGTGATGCTGATAGTGATGAGCTACTGG-3' and reverse: 5'-GAAGCCTTTGATGTGAAGAGGTTC-3'. The PCR primers for codon usage-optimized human IFNα2 are: forward: 5'-CTGGAAGCCTGCGTGATCC-3' and reverse: 5'-CTTGCAGGTTGGTGCTCAG-3'. The annealing temperature for codon usage-optimized DNA templates is 65°C.

sec.title: ELISA of mouse and human IFNα2 protein
sec.p: To measure mouse IFNα2 protein levels in serum and tumor lysates of mouse tumor-bearing syngeneic mice, an ELISA assay kit (Abcam, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA, cat# ab211648) was used. Tumor tissues were lysed in cell lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 7.4, 20 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1% Triton X-100) and the lysates were used for ELISA. To measure human IFNα2 protein levels in serum of human tumor-bearing humanized mice, we used an ELISA assay kit (BioLegend, California, USA, cat# 446407). ELISAs were carried out according to the manufacturer’s protocol. In brief, 50 µl of diluted sample was used per well of the precoated ELISA plate. For detection of IFNα2 in tumor-bearing tissue lysates, standards were additionally mixed with a lysis buffer to achieve the same final concentration of the lysis buffer between samples and standards. After incubation for 1 hour with the detection antibody cocktail, plates were washed 3× with 250 µl of wash buffer and 100 µl of 3, 3', 5, 5' tetramethyl benzidine (TMB) development solution was added to each well for 25 min. At the end, Stop Solution was added and absorbance at 450 nm was read using a microplate reader. IFNα2 concentration was calculated using the R package installed on R V.3.6.1 (https://www.r-project.org/). The limit of detection was calculated as an average of background samples plus 3×SD.

sec.title: LEGENDplex cytokines detection
sec.p: Detection of cytokines in serum and tumor lysates was performed using LEGENDplex Mouse Inflammation Panel (IFN-γ, interleukin (IL)-1α, IL-1β, IL-17A, granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), IL-23, IL-27; BioLegend Cat# 740446), or Mouse Proinflammatory Chemokine Panel V.02 (custom 2-plex set for CXCL9 and CXCL10; BioLegend Cat# 741295) according to manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, serum samples were diluted twofold with Assay Buffer and standards were mixed with Matrix Solution. For measurements in cell lysates, samples were diluted 4× with Assay Buffer and standards were appropriately mixed with the Lysis Buffer. Standards and samples were plated with capture beads and incubated overnight at 4°C on plate shaker. After washing the plate, detection antibodies were added to each well and the plate was incubated on shaker (600 rpm) for 1 hour at room temperature. Finally, without washing, Streptavidin-Phycoerythrin(PE) was added and incubated for 30 min. Samples were acquired on Novocyte Quanteon flow cytometer (Agilent Technologies). Standard curves and protein concentration were calculated using R package installed on R V.3.6.1. The limit of detection was calculated as an average of background samples plus 3×SD. Assay and data calculations were performed at Georgia Cancer Center Immune Monitoring Shared Resource laboratory.

sec.title: Cxcl9 neutralization
sec.p: 4T1 cells (2×104 cells/mouse) were injected into the mammary gland of mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated on day 10 after tumor cell injection with LNP (n=10) and LNP-mIFNα2 (n=19), respectively. The LNP-mIFNα2-treated tumor-bearing mice were divided into two groups and treated with IgG (n=10, 200 µg/mouse) or anti-Cxcl9 mAb (Clone MIG-2F5.5, Bio X Cell) (n=9, 200 µg/mouse) every 3 days for six times. B16-F10 cells (5×105 cells/mouse) were injected into tail veins of mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated 3 days after tumor cell injection with LNP (n=5) and LNP-mIFNα2 (n=9), respectively. The LNP-mIFNα2-treated tumor-bearing mice were divided into two groups and treated with IgG (n=5, 200 µg/mouse) and anti-Cxcl9 mAb (n=4, 200 µg/mouse) every 3 days for four times.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data was imported to GraphPad Prism V.10.2.2 to generate column plots. For groups of two, an F test to compare variance was run concurrently with a student parametric t test to calculate p value. For groups of three or more, a Bartlett’s test to compare variance was run concurrently with an ordinary one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by a multiple comparisons test to calculate p value. Specific multiple comparisons tests for ANOVAs are specified in figure legends. All statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism V.10.2.2. p<0.05 is considered to be significant. Unless specified otherwise, columns are mean±SD.

sec.title: IFN-I expression level is lost in tumor-infiltrating immune cells in human patients with cancer
sec.p: IFN-I signaling is often inhibited due to downregulated IFNAR1 and loss of IFN signaling leads to an immune-privileged niche in human tumors.24 To assess the expression profiles of the ligands for IFNAR1 in human cancer, we analyzed the expression of IFNα and IFNβ at the single-cell level in human patients with cancer. scRNA-Seq datasets of human patients with melanoma cancer25 were extracted and analyzed for the expression level of all IFNα isoforms, IFNβ1, and the IFN-I receptors (IFNAR1 and IFNAR2) in the major cell types. IFNA5 and IFNΑ22p are expressed in all major cell types, although at low levels in a small portion of cells (online supplemental figure S1A). All IFNα isoforms, except IFNA14, are expressed in T cells at a low level in a small fraction of cells. Other IFNα isoforms are expressed in various cell types (online supplemental figure S1A). IFNβ1 is expressed in endothelial cells. In contrast, IFNAR1 is expressed in cancer-associated fibroblasts, macrophages, and endothelial cells, whereas IFNAR2 is expressed in macrophages, T cells, and endothelial cells (online supplemental figure S1A). In human patients with breast cancer,26 only IFNΑ2, IFNA5, and IFNB1 are detectable in a small portion of tumor-infiltrating cells and their expression level is low (online supplemental figure S1B). IFNΑ2 is expressed in myeloid cell subset plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC), IFNA5 is expressed in a T cell subset, and IFNB1 is myeloid cell subsets and tumor cells (online supplemental figure S1B). Taken together, these findings indicate that IFN-I expression is limited to a very small fraction of cells and the expression level is low in cells that express it.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mouse IFNα2-encoding plasmid targets lungs in tumor-bearing mouse and produces IFNα2 protein in the tumor tissues
sec.p: Tumor cells use PD-L1 to engage myeloid cell PD-1 and activate SHP2 to repress IFN-I expression and signaling in myeloid cells to promote tumor immune evasion.7 Our above findings suggest that IFN-I expression is repressed in tumor-infiltrating cells in human patients with cancer. These findings provide a rationale for restoring IFN-I expression to reverse immune suppression in lung metastases niche. All IFNα2 isoforms and IFNβ function through binding to the same IFNAR1 and IFNAR2 dimer complex. IFNα2 recombinant protein is an FDA-approved immunotherapeutic agent for human cancer.8 We took this regulatory advantage and designed a codon usage-optimized DNA sequence (online supplemental figure S2). This DNA sequence encodes the full-length mouse IFNα2 protein (online supplemental figure S2).

This mouse codon usage-optimized IFNα2-encoding DNA was then cloned to nanoplasmid NCT9385R27 to create NTC9385R-mIFNα2 vector (online supplemental figure S3A). NTC9385R-mIFNα2 vector was then encapsulated in LNP DOTAP-cholesterol (online supplemental figure S3B) to generate LNP-encapsulated NTC9385R-mIFNα2 (LNP-mIFNα2) using our established procedures (online supplemental figure S3C and table S2).18 19 A pair of PCR primers were designed to selectively amplify the codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2-encoding DNA (online supplemental figure S3D), but not the endogenous mouse IFNα2 DNA. The activated T cells and mouse lung tissues were used as controls, respectively (online supplemental figure S3E–G). NTC9385R-mIFNα2 effectively transfected mouse tumor cells and expressed mouse IFNα2 in tumor cells in vitro (online supplemental figure S3H).

To determine LNP-mIFNα2 biodistribution in tumor-bearing mice, 4T1 tumor cells were injected intravenously to mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated with LNP-mIFNα2 and the major mouse organs were analyzed for the codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2 expression by PCR. The codon usage-optimized IFNα2 mRNA was detected in the tumor-bearing lungs in all three mice analyzed and in the intestine of one of the three mice (figure 1A). In the spontaneous 4T1 breast tumor mouse models, LNP-mIFNα2 therapy leads to expression of codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2 in the primary tumor (figure 1B) and IFNα2 protein production in the serum (figure 1C). Complementing this, in our 4T1 experimental lung metastasis model, IFNα2 protein is detected in serum and the tumor-bearing lungs after LNP-mIFNα2 therapy (figure 1D,E).

caption.title: LNP-mIFNα2 immune gene therapy produces IFNα2 protein in tumor lung metastases in vivo. (A) 4T1 cells (2×104 cells/mouse) were injected intravenously into BALB/c mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated once with LNP-mIFNα2 (n=3) 14 days after tumor cell injection. The indicated tissues were collected 3 days later and analyzed for IFNα2 mRNA by codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2 sequence-specific PCR. (B) 4T1 cells (2×104 cells/mouse) were injected into the mammary gland of the mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated 10 days later with LNP (n=10) or LNP-mIFNα2 (n=10) every 7 days for four times. Primary tumors were dissected from mice 1 day after the last treatment and analyzed for codon usage optimized mouse IFNα2 mRNA level by PCR. (C) Sera were collected from the tumor-bearing mice as in B and analyzed for mIFNα2 protein level by mouse IFNα2-specific ELISA. LOD: limit of detection. (D) 4T1 cells (2×104 cells/mouse) were injected into the tail vein of mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated 14 days later with LNP (n=5) and LNP-mIFNα2 (n=4) every 7 days for 2 times. Sera were collected 3 days after the last treatment and analyzed for mouse IFNα2 protein using mouse IFNα2-specific ELISA. (E) 4T1 cells were injected into the tail vein of mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated 14 days later with LNP (n=5) and LNP-mIFNα2 (n=5) every 7 days for 2 times. Tumor-bearing lungs were collected 3 days after the last treatment and prepared for total protein lysate. The total protein lysates were analyzed for mouse IFNα2 protein using mouse IFNα2-specific ELISA. LNP-mIFNα2, lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mouse IFNα2; mRNA, messenger RNA.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered IFNα2 increases T cell-attracting chemokine production to enhance T cell tumor infiltration in tumor-bearing mice
sec.p: Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 are essential CTL recruitment chemokines produced by myeloid cells in human patients with cancer.2830 Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 expressions are regulated by IFN-I and are repressed by the PD-(L)1 immunosuppressive pathway in myeloid cells in tumor-bearing mice.7 Consistent with these findings, Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 levels are low in tumor-bearing mice and LNP-mIFNα2 therapy significantly increased Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 protein levels in the tumor-bearing mice (figure 2A). Increased Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 protein levels are correlated with a significantly increased level of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in lung metastases in LNP-mIFNα2-treated mice (figure 2B,C). Furthermore, the level of IFNγ, a T cell activation marker, is also significantly increased in LNP-mIFNα2-treated tumor-bearing mice (figure 2D). Taken together, our findings determine that LNP-mIFNα2 is effective in restoring IFNα2 expression to reactivate IFN-I signaling to upregulate the expression of Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 to enhance T cell recruitment and activation in lung metastases in vivo.

caption.title: LNP-mIFNα2 therapy restores IFNα2 expression to activate T cell chemokine and IFNγ production in tumor-bearing mice. (A) 4T1 cells (2×104 cells/mouse) were injected into tail veins of mice. The tumor-bearing mice were treated 14 days later with LNP (n=5) and LNP-mIFNα2 (n=5), respectively, every 7 days for two times. Sera were collected 3 days after the last treatment and analyzed by the custom 2-plex Mouse Panel of two beads detecting Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 protein. (B and C) Tumor-bearing mouse lungs were analyzed for T cell level by flow cytometry. Shown are dot plots of T cells in 5 mice (B) and T cell quantification (C). (D) IFNγ protein level in tumor-bearing mouse serum as in A. (E) Proinflammatory cytokine level in the tumor-bearing mice as in A. GM-CSF, granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor; IFNγ, interferon-gamma; IL, interleukin; LNP-mIFNα2, lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mouse IFNα2.

sec.title: LNP-mIFNα2 therapy does not induce a proinflammatory response in tumor-bearing mice
sec.p: A common side effect of LNP-based therapy is a cytokine storm, as characterized by release of the proinflammatory cytokines.31 32 To determine the toxicity of LNP-mIFNα2, we measured a panel of proinflammatory cytokines, including IL1α, IL1β, IL17A, TNFα, IL23, IL27, and GM-CSF. LNP-mIFNα2 therapy significantly decreased IL23 level, but the levels of other cytokines were not significantly changed by LNP-mIFNα2 therapy (figure 2E).

sec.title: LNP-mIFNα2 effectively suppresses tumor lung metastasis in tumor-bearing mice
sec.p: To determine the efficacy of LNP-mIFNα2 in suppression of tumor lung metastasis, the spontaneous lung metastasis 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were treated with LNP-mIFNα2 and analyzed for tumor growth and lung metastasis. LNP-mIFNα2 therapy significantly suppressed the primary tumor growth as measured by tumor size. However, the tumor weight is not significant between the LNP control group and the LNP-mIFNα2 treatment group (figure 3A–C). Analysis of lung metastasis revealed that all mice developed lung metastases in the control group, but only 20% (2 of 10) of the mice developed lung metastases in the LNP-mIFNα2 treatment group. Furthermore, quantification of lung metastases nodule number indicates that LNP-mIFNα2 therapy significantly decreased lung metastasis in this breast cancer spontaneous lung metastasis mouse model (figure 3D,E). To further determine the efficacy of LNP-mIFNα2 on suppression of lung metastasis, we injected 4T1 tumor cells intravenously into mice to establish lung metastasis. LNP-mIFNα2 therapy significantly increased survival of the tumor-bearing mice in this breast cancer experimental lung metastasis mouse model (figure 3F).

sec.p: The B16F10 melanoma experimental lung metastasis mouse model was then used as a complementary model to determine the efficacy of LNP-mIFNα2. B16F10 cells were injected into C57BL/6 mice intravenously to establish lung metastasis. Treatment of the tumor-bearing mice with LNP-mIFNα2 significantly decreased lung metastases nodule number (figure 3G,H). Histological analysis of mouse lungs indicated widespread lung metastases and LNP-mIFNα2 therapy suppressed lung metastasis (figure 3I,J).

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle delivery of IFNα2 mRNA suppresses tumor lung metastasis in tumor-bearing mice
sec.p: LNP delivery of mRNA has shown effectiveness in expressing a functional protein to suppress tumor development in tumor-bearing mice in vivo.3335 To determine whether the LNP is effective in encapsulating and delivering IFNα2-encoding mRNA to produce functional IFNα2 protein to suppress tumor lung metastasis, we synthesized mRNA from the codon usage-optimized mouse IFNα2-encoding DNA (online supplemental figure S2). The mRNA was encapsulated in DOTAP-cholesterol to generate LNP-encapsulated mouse IFNα2 mRNA (termed LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA) (online supplemental table S2). Primary tumor with spontaneous lung metastasis 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were treated with LNP or varying doses of LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA, respectively. LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA at a dose of 5 µg mRNA/mouse significantly suppressed primary tumor growth (figure 4A) and the spontaneous lung metastasis (figure 4B). Furthermore, LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA at a dose of 5 µg mRNA/mouse also significantly suppressed melanoma lung metastasis in the experimental melanoma lung metastasis mouse model (figure 4C). Analysis of the B16-F10 tumor-bearing mouse lungs revealed that LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA therapy produced mouse IFNα2 protein in the lung metastases tissues (figure 4D). Mouse IFNα2 protein is also significantly increased in the tumor-bearing mouse serum after LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA therapy (figure 4E). Consistent with increased IFNα2, Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 protein levels are also significantly increased in the treated mice (figure 4F). IFNγ level increased after LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA treatment, although not statistically significant (figure 4G). Taken together, these findings determine that LNP delivery of IFNα2-encoding plasmid DNA and mRNA produces functional IFNα2 protein in the tumor-bearing mice to effectively suppress tumor lung metastasis.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle delivery of human IFNα2-encoding plasmid restores human IFNα2 expression to suppress human tumor lung metastasis
sec.p: To translate the above finding to human cancer therapy, we designed codon usage-optimized human IFNα2-encoding DNA (online supplemental figure S4). This DNA sequence encodes the full-length human IFNα2 protein (online supplemental figure S4). This human codon usage-optimized IFNα2-encoding DNA was then cloned to nanoplasmid NCT9385R27 to create NTC9385R-hIFNα2 vector (figure 5A). NTC9385R-hIFNα2 plasmid DNA was then encapsulated into DOTAP-cholesterol to generate LNP-encapsulated NTC9385R-hIFNα2 (LNP-hIFNα2) using our established procedures (figure 5B) (online supplemental table S2).18 19 A pair of PCR primers was then designed to selectively amplify the codon usage-optimized human IFNα2-coding DNA. NTC9385R-hIFNα2 vector can effectively transfect human tumor cells and express codon usage-optimized human IFNα2 in human tumor cells in vitro (figure 5C).

sec.p: To determine the efficacy of LNP-hIFNα2 in suppression of human tumor metastasis, NSG mice were humanized using human PBMCs using our established procedures.18 The humanized mice were then injected with human colon tumor cells intravenously to establish experimental lung metastases. The human tumor-bearing humanized mice were treated with LNP-hIFNα2 (figure 5D). ELISA analysis revealed that LNP-hIFNα2-treated mice produce human IFNα2 protein (figure 5E) and LNP-hIFNα2 therapy significantly decreased lung metastases nodule number in the human tumor-bearing humanized mice (figure 5F).

sec.title: LNP-mIFNα2 has no significant adverse effect in tumor-bearing mice
sec.p: To assess the toxicity of LNP-mIFNα2, spontaneous lung metastasis 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were monitored for body weight change after LNP-mIFNα2 treatment. LNP-mIFNα2 therapy resulted in less than 10% body weight change as compared with LNP control over a 19-day period (online supplemental figure S5). The liver enzyme profiles, particularly the levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and alkaline phosphatase (ALP), are considered key indicators of liver damage and thus liver toxicity.36 Analysis of mouse serum indicates that LNP-mIFNα2 treatment decreased albumin level but did not cause a significant change in ALP and ALT level in mouse tumor-bearing syngeneic mice (online supplemental figure S6A). Mouse and human IFN-I functions are interactive in mouse and human.37 Analysis of human tumor-bearing humanized NSG mice indicates that LNP-hIFNα2 did not cause a significant change in albumin, ALP, and ALT level (online supplemental figure S6B).

Analysis of a panel of inflammatory cytokines of tumor-bearing mouse serum revealed that LNP-mIFNα2-encoding mRNA therapy significantly increased IL1β protein level (online supplemental figure S7). The levels of GM-CSF, IL1α, IL17A, TNFα, IL23, and IL27 were not significantly changed in LNP-mIFNα2-mRNA-treated mice (online supplemental figure S7).

sec.title: IFN-I signaling pathway is associated with Cxcl9 expression and patient with cancer response to PD-(L)1 inhibitor immunotherapy
sec.p: To determine the human cancer relevance of the mechanism of action of IFN-I, we analyzed human patients with cancer scRNA-Seq datasets.20 In human patients with breast cancer, pembrolizumab immunotherapy induced T cell expansion in a portion of patients (figure 6A). Patients who responded to pembrolizumab with T cell expansion also have IFN-I signature activation in immune cells, primarily in myeloid cells (figure 6B,C). IFN-I signature activation is also correlated with increased CXCL9 expression in myeloid cells in these responsive patients (figure 6D,E). Similarly, in human patients with melanoma, pembrolizumab immunotherapy activates IFN-I signature in immune cells, particularly in myeloid cells (figure 6F–J). Pembrolizumab-induced IFN-I signature activation is also associated with increased CXCL9 expression in myeloid cells (figure 6K–M). These findings indicate that PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy reactivates IFN-I signature to activate Cxcl9 expression to increase T cell tumor infiltration.

sec.title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered IFNα2 activates Cxcl9 expression to recruit T cells into the tumor microenvironment to suppress tumor lung metastasis
sec.p: CXCL9 is a T cell chemokine that is produced by myeloid cells and functions to recruit T cells into the tumor site in human patients with cancer.283038 In addition, patients with more CXCL9hi tumor-associated macrophages had better clinical outcomes and CXCL9hi tumor-associated macrophage is a better prognostic biomarker than the M1 and M2 macrophages.29 CXCL9 is an IFN-I target gene7 and it is reasonable that IFNα2 may regulate Cxcl9 expression. We therefore aimed at testing the hypothesis that LNP-IFNα2 therapy suppresses tumor lung metastasis through restoring IFNα2 expression to activate Cxcl9 to increase T cell tumor recruitment. To test this hypothesis, spontaneous lung metastasis 4T1 tumor-bearing mice were treated with LNP-mIFNα2, followed by treatment with anti-Cxcl9 mAb. While Cxcl9 blockade exhibited minimal effect on the primary tumor growth (figure 7A,B), it diminished the efficacy of LNP-mIFNα2 in suppression of breast tumor lung metastasis (figure 7C). Similarly, Cxcl9 blockade diminished the efficacy of LNP-mIFNα2 in suppression of melanoma lung metastasis in the B16F10 melanoma experimental lung metastasis mouse model (figure 7D,E). Analysis of the tumor tissues determined that Cxcl9 blockade suppressed LNP-mIFNα2-induced increase of CD8+ T cells in the lung metastases (figure 7F,G). Taken together, these findings determine that LNP delivery of IFNα2 enhances T cell tumor recruitment to suppress tumor lung metastasis in part by activating Cxcl9 expression and production.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The first and second generation of IFN-I agents are IFNα2 recombinant proteins that are associated with severe adverse effects. A new type of IFN-I was engineered by masking IFN-Fc protein to target tumor site for tumor cell protease-dependent release of the cargo IFN-Fc protein to increase the half-life and to reduce toxicity.14 However, the active agent is still exogenous recombinant IFN-I protein. The stimulator of interferon genes (STING) agonists have emerged as a promising class of immunotherapeutic agents for inducing robust antitumor immunity in tumor-bearing mice and human patients with cancer.3942 Toxicity associated with systemic immune activation and tumor site-selective delivery remains a challenge for STING agonists.42 The success of LNP-encapsulated COVID-19 mRNA vaccine opened a new avenue for delivering peptide/protein-encoding nucleic acid to target site to produce functional endogenous peptides/proteins in the host.15 The DNA-encoding protein is continuously expressed and likely post-translationally modified in the same way as the genome-encoded endogenous protein, thereby overcoming the short half-life and activity issues with the exogenous recombinant protein. In this study, we determined that LNP-IFNα2 therapy produces endogenous IFNα2 protein and suppresses tumor lung metastasis in mice. LNP-IFNα2 is therefore potentially a third generation of IFNα2 agent.

DOTAP nanoparticle primarily accumulates in the lung, liver, and spleen in mice.43 Adding a cationic helper lipid, such as cholesterol, to an LNP can increase lung delivery and decrease liver targeting.44 DOTAP-cholesterol-encapsulated plasmid DNA therapy in human patients with lung cancer leads to a 10–25 folds increase of the plasmid-encoded tumor suppressor protein in the lung tumor tissues, but not in the peripheral lymphocytes in patients with cancer.16 It is known that the actively proliferating cells, such as tumor cells, are more likely to take up plasmid DNA than the slowly dividing normal cells through endocytosis to transfer the plasmid DNA inside the cells to express the encoded protein.45 In this study, we observed that DOTAP-cholesterol-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid liposome predominantly targets tumor-bearing lungs. Our findings indicate that, in addition to the helper lipid cholesterol, the encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid DNA may further increase DOTAP-cholesterol selectivity for the tumor-bearing lungs. It is likely that DOTAP-cholesterol-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid liposome (LNP-IFNα2) therapy selectively targets tumor cells in the lung metastases niche to force tumor cells to express and produce active endogenous IFNα2 protein. The cell types that take up plasmid DNA and mRNA-encapsulated LNP in the tumor lung metastases-bearing lungs remain to be determined and warrant further study. Nevertheless, our findings determine that LPN-IFNα2 selectively targets tumor-bearing lungs to produce active endogenous IFNα2 protein to suppress tumor lung metastasis.

Chemokines play essential roles as attractants of naïve and effector T cells. CXCL9 and CXCL10 are macrophage-produced CTL-attracting chemokines and are essential for CTL tumor recruitment in human patients with cancer.28 30 However, only CXCL9 expression level in macrophages is positively associated with increased tumor infiltration of T cells and a better prognosis.29 Cxcl9 is a downstream target gene of IFN-I.7 In this study, we determined that LNP-IFNα2 therapy produces IFNα2 protein and increases Cxcl9 protein level in tumor-bearing mice. Furthermore, Cxcl9 neutralization decreased tumor-infiltrating CTL level and LNP-IFNα2 efficacy in suppression of tumor lung metastasis in mice. Our findings therefore determine that LNP-IFNα2 suppresses tumor lung metastasis at least in part through activating Cxcl9 expression to increase CTL tumor recruitment in the lung metastases niche.

STING agonists induce IFN-I expression to induce antitumor immunity.394146 In addition to IFN-I expression induction, STING agonists also activate proinflammatory cytokines, which may lead to toxicity.42 A side effect of LNP-based therapy is the cytokine syndrome as characterized by release of the proinflammatory cytokines.31 32 In this study, DOTAP-cholesterol-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid liposome did not increase proinflammatory cytokines in tumor-bearing mice. However, DOTAP-cholesterol-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding mRNA significantly increased IL1β protein level in tumor-bearing mice, suggesting potential toxicity of LNP-IFNα2-mRNA therapy. The mechanism underlying the different proinflammatory cytokine profiles between DOTAP-cholesterol-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid and DOTAP-cholesterol-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding mRNA is not clear and requires further study.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Lung metastases are the second most common metastatic disease for patients with cancer and occur in approximately 30% of patients with cancer with metastatic cancer. Patients with lung metastases have a short survival time.47 The recent findings that tumor cells use PD-L1 to engage myeloid cell PD-1 to activate SHP2 to antagonize IFN-I to repress Cxcl9 and impair CTL recruitment in lung metastases7 and the critical function of IFN-I in antitumor immunity and suppression of tumor lung metastasis143941 48 indicate that loss of IFN-I underlies tumor immune evasion in lung metastases niche. Pharmacological means to restore IFN-I and function is therefore potentially an effective approach for lung metastasis therapy. Recombinant IFNα2 is an FDA-approved agent for human cancer. However, its toxicity limits its clinical use.12 13 In this study, we determine that LNP-encapsulated IFNα2-encoding plasmid primarily targets lung tissues and effectively produces IFNα2 protein to activate Cxcl9 to increase CTL tumor recruitment to suppress lung metastasis without significant toxicity. LNP-IFNα2 is therefore potentially a third generation of IFN-I agent for lung metastases immunotherapy.
